                                                                   Stable isotopy in four dimensions

                                                     Dave Auckly, Hee Jung Kim, Paul Melvin and Daniel Ruberman




arXiv:1406.4937v2 [math.GT] 11 Nov 2014
                                                                                      Abstract
                                            We construct infinite families of topologically isotopic but smoothly distinct knotted spheres in
                                            many simply-connected 4-manifolds that become smoothly isotopic after stabilizing by connected
                                            summing with S 2 ˆS 2 , and as a consequence, analogous families of diffeomorphisms and metrics
                                            of positive scalar curvature for such 4-manifolds. We also construct families of smoothly distinct
                                            links, all of whose corresponding proper sublinks are smoothly isotopic, that become smoothly
                                            isotopic after stabilizing.



                                                                                    1. Introduction
                                             A basic principle of smooth 4-dimensional topology due to Wall [67] is that homotopy
                                          equivalent, simply-connected 4-manifolds become diffeomorphic after connected summing with
                                          sufficiently many copies of S 2 ˆS 2 . In fact the same result holds for any pair of orientable
                                          homeomorphic 4-manifolds [37, 48]. The process of summing with a single S 2 ˆS 2 is called
                                          stabilization. The number of stabilizations needed to obtain a diffeomorphism is not known in
                                          general, although it follows from the existence of exotic smooth structures (see [26, 28] and
                                          many subsequent papers) that at least one stabilization is often required. In fact exactly one
                                          stabilization suffices for many important families of examples (see for example [57, 4, 15]), and
                                          surprisingly, no examples have been found that require more than one (see [27, 29, 11] for an
                                          approach to this question). Thus one might reasonably speculate that any pair of homeomorphic
                                          simply-connected 4-manifolds become diffeomorphic after a single stabilization. Indeed this has
                                          been shown to be the case for all odd (i.e. nonspin) pairs produced using ‘standard methods’
                                          (logarithmic transforms, knot surgeries, and rational blow downs) and thus also for all even
                                          pairs after an initial ‘blowup’ (see below) [16].
                                             This paper explores analogous stabilization questions for smoothly embedded 2-spheres in
                                          4-manifolds, and for ambient diffeomorphisms derived from such spheres. For example, it follows
                                          from Wall [66] and the work of Perron [59] and Quinn [60] that any pair of 2-spheres embedded
                                          with simply-connected complements in a 4-manifold that represent the same homology class are
                                          topologically isotopic, and they become smoothly isotopic after some number of stabilizations.
                                          Again it is reasonable to ask for bounds on that number. In this setting, however, no bounds
                                          have been established (before now) for any explicit examples. We will produce infinite families of
                                          knotted spheres that require exactly one stabilization to become isotopic (henceforth ‘isotopic’
                                          will mean ‘smoothly isotopic’ unless stated otherwise) and analogous pairs of links of arbitrarily
                                          many components all of whose corresponding proper sublinks are isotopic.
                                             With regard to diffeomorphisms of 4-manifolds, the appropriate notion of stabilization is to
                                          take the connected sum with the identity map on S 2 ˆS 2 , explained in more detail below. In
                                          [60], Quinn showed that homotopic diffeomorphisms of any simply-connected 4-manifold are
                                          stably isotopic, again raising the question of how many stabilizations are necessary. Here we



                                           2000 Mathematics Subject Classification 57M25 (primary), 57Q60 (secondary).
                                            Kim was supported by NRF grants 2012R1A1A2006981 and BK21 PLUS SNU Mathematical Sciences
                                          Division. Ruberman was partially supported by NSF Grant 1105234 and NSF FRG Grant 1065827
Page 2 of 25                AUCKLY, KIM, MELVIN AND RUBERMAN



construct examples of infinite families for which exactly one stabilization is needed, and in
a similar vein, examples of non-isotopic Riemannian metrics of positive scalar curvature that
become isotopic after one stabilization.
  We make the following definitions to capture these questions:

  Definition. Two simply-connected 4-manifolds X and Y are n-stably equivalent if
                                X # nS 2 ˆS 2 – Y # nS 2 ˆS 2
(where we write nZ for the connected sum of n copies of Z, and – denotes orientation preserving
diffeomorphism) and strictly n-stably equivalent, written X –n Y , if they are n-stably but
not pn ´ 1q-stably equivalent. There are analogous definitions for stabilizations with other
manifolds Z in place of S 2 ˆS 2 (typically Z “ ˘CP2 or S 2 r̂ S 2 ), with the corresponding strict
equivalence denoted X –n Y (mod Z), but to avoid confusion here we will reserve the term
‘stabilization’ for # S 2 ˆS 2 .
   Similarly, two embedded 2-spheres S , T Ă X (resp. diffeomorphisms f , g : X Ñ X) are
n-stably isotopic if the natural embeddings S , T Ă X # nS 2 ˆS 2 are isotopic (resp. the
connected sums of f and g with the identity map 11 on nS 2 ˆS 2 are isotopic; this connected
sum is shown to be well-defined up to isotopy in section 5; compare [36]). There is also a
weaker notion of n-stable equivalence, requiring only the existence of a diffeomorphisms σ and
τ of X # nS 2 ˆS 2 such that T “ σpSq (resp. g # 11 “ τ ˝ pf # 11q ˝ σ). The notions of strict
n-stable isotopy and equivalence are defined in the obvious way. We note the simple fact that
the notions of n-stable isotopy and equivalence are actually equivalence relations.

   With this terminology, the principal goal of this paper is to produce explicit examples of
strictly 1-stably isotopic embeddings of spheres in simply-connected 4-manifolds, and thereby
to produce strictly 1-stably isotopic diffeomorphisms of related manifolds. The emphasis is on
the word ‘explicit’, for the existence of such examples follows directly from the existence of
n-stably isotopic spheres that are not smoothly isotopic. The issue is that one has no a priori
control on n. We gain this control by working locally, within a blown-up cork (as explained in
section 3), thereby producing explicit examples of strictly 1-stably isotopic 2-spheres in large
families of ‘simple’ 4-manifolds.
   Before proceeding, recall that blowing up an oriented 4-manifold X refers to the process of
connected summing with ˘CP2 . The effect is to replace a point in X with an embedded
2-sphere ˘CP1 , the exceptional sphere of the blowup. The choice of orientation on CP2
naturally affects the outcome, detected by the signature. Using `CP2 yields the positive blowup
X ` , and using ´CP2 (also commonly written CP2 ) yields its negative blowup X ´ :
                          X ` “ X # CP2        and X ´ “ X # CP2
This terminology is borrowed from the theory of complex surfaces, where one blows up a point
by replacing it with the projective line – or exceptional curve – of complex tangent lines through
that point, which in this case has self-intersection ´1. Thus the complex blowup corresponds
to the negative topological blowup; as a result, some topologists prefer to call X ´ the blowup
of X, and X ` its antiblowup, but we do not do so here. Note that if one restricts to blowups of
the same sign, then there are many examples of homeomorphic 4-manifolds that never become
diffeomorphic no matter how many times they are blown up. To achieve the analogue of Wall’s
stabilization result, one needs to allow blowups of both signs. Indeed, it is well known that
X `´ – X # S 2 ˆS 2 when X is odd, and so an equal number of positive and negative blowups
will eventually yield diffeomorphic manifolds.
   Conversely, one can blow down an embedded 2-sphere S of self intersection ˘1 in a 4-manifold
X. The result will be denoted by X{S since, topologically, it is the quotient space obtained by
collapsing S to a point. For example X “ X ˘ {S ˘ , where S ˘ is the exceptional sphere in X ˘ .
                             STABLE ISOTOPY IN FOUR DIMENSIONS                        Page 3 of 25


  The embedded spheres (and related diffeomorphisms and metrics) constructed in this paper
to illustrate 1-stability all live in the family of completely decomposable 4-manifolds

                                     Xp,q :“ pCP2 # qCP2

obtained from S 4 by p positive and q negative blowups.


  Theorem A. If p ě 4 is even and q ě 5p, then Xp,q contains an infinite family tSk | k ě 0u
of topologically isotopic embedded 2-spheres that are pairwise strictly 1-stably isotopic, i.e.
smoothly isotopic in Xp,q # S 2 ˆS 2 but not in Xp,q . For q ě 9, X2,q contains a pair S, T of
topologically isotopic spheres that are strictly 1-stably isotopic


   In fact all the spheres we construct have self-intersection `1, and their blowdowns have
distinct Seiberg-Witten invariants. Hence they are not only smoothly nonisotopic, but a fortiori
smoothly inequivalent, i.e. no diffeomorphism of Xp,q carries any one to any other.
   Our examples arise naturally, illustrating a close relation between 1-stable equivalence of
manifolds modulo CP2 and inequivalence of spheres of self-intersection `1: Start with a pair of
4-manifolds X –1 Y (mod CP2 ), i.e. X fl Y but X ` – Y ` . Let S be the exceptional sphere in
X ` , and T be the image of the exceptional sphere in Y ` under any diffeomorphism Y ` Ñ X ` .
Then S and T are inequivalent in X ` . The harder task is to produce examples that are strictly
1-stably isotopic, i.e. isotopic in X ` # S 2 ˆS 2 (also see Section 1 below). We accomplish this by
localizing our construction: There are pairs of strictly 1-stably isotopic spheres in the blowup
W ` of a certain contractible 4-manifold W , the Akbulut-Mazur cork (see Section 3) which has
the needed properties to produce the infinite family of spheres in Theorem A. In fact, W is the
first of an infinite family of corks with these same properties, each producing infinite families
of spheres (see Section 3). To extend the result when p “ 2 to produce an infinite family of
spheres, it would be sufficient to find a suitable embedding of such a cork in X1,9 .
   Theorem A extends to a stabilization result for links of spheres in 4-manifolds. The links we
find come in families that satisfy a property reminiscent of Brunnian links [20, 25] in that,
once suitably ordered, all their corresponding proper sublinks are smoothly isotopic. We will
refer to any such family of links as a Brunnian family.


  Theorem B. Fix m ą 1. If p ě 2 is even and q ě 5p ` 2 por q ě 11 when p “ 2q then
Xp`m´1,q contains a Brunnian pair of topologically isotopic m-component ordered links that
are strictly 1-stably isotopic. Furthermore, for p ě 4 there exists an infinite family of smoothly
distinct such m-component links.


   The spheres described in Theorem A in turn lead to examples of strictly 1-stably isotopic
diffeomorphisms by invoking a construction that dates back to early work of Wall [66], or even
earlier in Picard-Lefschetz theory [51]. The key observation is that an embedded sphere Σ of
self-intersection ˘1 or ˘2 in a 4-manifold X gives rise to a diffeomorphism of X, supported
in a neighborhood of Σ, that induces a ‘reflection’ in the second homology. An isotopy of such
2-spheres yields an isotopy of the corresponding diffeomorphisms, by the isotopy extension
theorem. Note that the converse of this statement is not known to be true in general, but it
holds ‘morally’: the non-isotopic diffeomorphisms constructed in [61, 62, 63] are compositions
of such reflections in spheres, and in the end are detected by gauge-theoretic invariants that
also show these spheres to be non-isotopic. Combining these results with Theorem A gives
1-stability of an infinite family of non-isotopic diffeomorphisms.
Page 4 of 25                AUCKLY, KIM, MELVIN AND RUBERMAN



  Theorem C. If p ě 4 is even and q ě 5p ` 2, then Xp,q supports an infinite family
tfk : Xp,qœ  | k ě 0u of topologically isotopic self-diffeomorphisms that are pairwise strictly
1-stably isotopic, i.e. not smoothly isotopic, but such that the diffeomorphisms fk # idS2ˆS2 of
Xp,q # S 2 ˆS 2 are all smoothly isotopic.


   We will show that the stabilization f ÞÑ f # idS2ˆS2 is in fact well-defined on isotopy
classes of (orientation preserving) diffeomorphisms, and hence induces a homomorphism
Φ : π0 pDiff pM qq Ñ π0 pDiff pM # S 2 ˆS 2 qq. From this, we will deduce that for Xp,q as in
Theorem C, the kernel of Φ is infinite.

  Remark. Versions of theorems A and C are likely to hold for other families of simply-
connected closed manifolds. For Xp,q when p is odd, this would require the use of gauge theory
invariants for manifolds with even b`
                                    2 , and in general would require a better understanding of
the exotic smooth structures on other manifolds.

   The fact that the diffeomorphisms fk in Theorem C are not isotopic is detected by
parameterized versions of the Donaldson and Seiberg-Witten invariants [61, 63] that work for
even p ě 4 (extending such invariants to the p “ 2 case is analogous to defining gauge theory
invariants when b`2 “ 1). Now the manifolds Xp,q admit metrics of positive scalar curvature
(PSC for short) constructed as the connected sum [41, 64] of standard metrics gF S on CP2
and CP2 . The 1-parameter version of the Seiberg-Witten invariants reveal an additional fact
about such metrics g, namely that the pull-back metrics fk˚ g, all of which have PSC, are not
isotopic to one another, where an isotopy is a 1-parameter family of PSC metrics. Connected
sum with a PSC metric on S 2 ˆS 2 then leads to a 1-stability result for such metrics.


  Theorem D. If p ě 4 is even and q ě 5p ` 2, then Xp,q admits an infinite family
tgk | k ě 0u of PSC metrics that are mutually non-isotopic. The metrics gk become isotopic
through PSC metrics after connected summing with the standard PSC metric on S 2 ˆS 2 .


  Remark. In contrast to the well-known stabilization theorems for simply-connected 4-
manifolds and diffeomorphisms, there does not seem to be a general stabilization result for
PSC metrics. The paper [19] (cf. also [68, 71]) would suggest that such a result ought to
hold, but at present there is a gap in one of the main geometric steps in [19]. Note that the
stabilization results for manifolds (under # S 2 ˆS 2 ) generalize to arbitrary closed oriented 4-
manifolds [37, 48], but fail for nonorientable 4-manifolds [21]. Similarly, orientability may be
essential for analogous results for PSC metrics. In particular, it seems likely that the metrics
constructed in [63, §6] remain non-isotopic, even up to diffeomorphism, after an arbitrary
number of stabilizations.

Stable diffeomorphism versus stable isotopy
   It is important to keep track of the distinction between equivalence of surfaces up to
diffeomorphism and up to isotopy, especially in applications to questions of stable isotopy
of diffeomorphisms and PSC metrics.
   For knots in S 3 , Cerf’s theorem [23] implies that the existence of an orientation preserving
diffeomorphism taking one knot to another yields an ambient isotopy accomplishing the same
thing. The analogous result (replacing orientation preserving with homotopic to the identity)
is not known to be true for surfaces in 4-manifolds. In fact we suspect that this is false. Thus,
any argument that does not produce an explicit isotopy at some point is unlikely to be a
                             STABLE ISOTOPY IN FOUR DIMENSIONS                        Page 5 of 25


valid argument showing that two surfaces in a 4-manifold are smoothly isotopic. Our proof of
Theorem A produces such an isotopy.
   In contrast, it is easy to construct pairs of spheres that are smoothly distinct, yet become
equivalent by an ambient diffeomorphism after one stabilization. Indeed, take any two distinct,
simply-connected, smooth 4-manifolds X and Y that are homeomorphic, but become diffeo-
morphic after summing with CP2 , and also with S 2 ˆS 2 . Then by choosing a diffeomorphism
f : Y # CP2 Ñ X # CP2 appropriately, one can assume that the spheres CP1 and f pCP1 q in
X # CP2 are topologically isotopic. These spheres are smoothly distinct in X # CP2 , since
a diffeomorphism taking one to the other would produce a diffeomorphism between X and
Y , by blowing down. Now for any diffeomorphism g : pS 2 ˆS 2 q # X Ñ pS 2 ˆS 2 q # Y , the
diffeomorphism
              p1 # f q ˝ pg # 1q : pS 2 ˆS 2 q # X # CP2 ÝÑ pS 2 ˆS 2 q # X # CP2
takes CP1 to f pCP1 q. There are a few subtle points here, since the connected sum of
diffeomorphisms is not generally well defined, but it is (as shown in Section 5) in the cases
above.
   The above argument does not say anything about the existence of an isotopy between CP1
and f pCP1 q in pS 2 ˆS 2 q # X # CP2 . We can arrange that p1 # f q ˝ pg # 1q is homotopic to the
identity, but it’s certainly not true in general that homotopy implies isotopy [61]. The point
of our work is that by looking more carefully one can actually see the isotopy.

  Acknowledgements. The authors discussed this material at conferences held at MSRI and
BIRS; we thank both institutes for their hospitality. We also thank Ryan Budney and Boris
Botvinnik for helpful comments on the material related to diffeomorphisms and positive scalar
curvature metrics. A key idea in our proof of Theorem A is to perform the stabilization inside
a cork. This localization leads to readily drawn pictures of non-isotopic spheres that from
other points of view would seem rather complicated and hard to work with. We are happy to
acknowledge the influence of Selman Akbulut’s cork-twisting technique on our approach to this
problem, and to thank him for some interesting exchanges on the subject (cf. [7]).


                                  2. Some basic constructions
  In this section, we discuss some constructions that will be used repeatedly in the proofs of
our main results.

Surfaces and handles
   Let Z be an oriented, compact connected 4-manifold with a fixed handle decomposition. We
view the 1-skeleton of Z as B 4 ´ N , where N is a union of unknotted, embedded open 2-handles
in B 4 attached along an unlink L in S 3 . In pictures, following a long-standing convention, we
put dots on the components of L to distinguish them from the attaching circles of the 2-handles
(see [46] or [40] for detailed expositions of 4-dimensional handle calculus). As an additional
notational convention, we will write hc for the 2-handle attached along a knot c in S 3 ´ L.
   An oriented surface F embedded in Z is described easily in terms of the given handle
decomposition (this is discussed in [9] and [40, §6.2] in some special cases): By transversality, we
can assume after an isotopy that F is disjoint from the 3 and 4-handles, intersects the 2-handles
in some number of parallel copies of their cores, and intersects the 1-handles in tubes and bands
that run parallel to their cores. The rest of F can be moved to a proper critical level embedding
in B 4 ´ N , with minima at radius 1{4, saddles at radius 1{2, and relative maxima at radius
3{4 (although maxima will not arise for surfaces considered here). By projecting back up to
radius 1, we see most of this surface immersed in S 3 ´ L with boundary consisting of framed
Page 6 of 25                    AUCKLY, KIM, MELVIN AND RUBERMAN



pushoffs of the attaching circles of the 2-handles and zero-pushoffs of the dotted circles, which
bound disks missing from our view. In pictures, rather than actually drawing the pushoffs
of these circles, we will extend the surface to abut them by adding a boundary collar. The
1-handles associated with the saddles, which we refer to as ribbons, will typically be shaded
darker (green) to remind us that they lie above the lighter (blue) regions around the minima.
  In the arguments below, we will need to carry F along as the handle decomposition of Z
changes by handle slides. The simplest non-trivial case occurs when a 2-handle ha disjoint from
F slides over a 2-handle hc that meets F , resulting in a new 2-handle ha1 . This is illustrated
in Figure 1. The handle hc and F are unchanged; the apparent intersection of a1 with F does
not occur since F is actually pushed into the 4-ball at that point.


                                      1

                                      c             slide
           a                                                           a1

                   Figure 1. Sliding a 2-handle over a 2-handle containing a surface


   By contrast, if ha meets F and hc does not, then sliding ha over hc will drag a portion of F
over hc , as indicated in Figure 2. We use Fc (read ‘F over c’) to denote this new picture of F
in the new handlebody, and refer to this as a surface-slide.

handle hc by the sliding the handles ha and hb that ‘bound’ the ribbon over hc , as shown in
Figure 3. We denote the resulting surface by Fcc , where the c denotes c with its orientation
reversed. This notation records the fact that the slides are oppositely oriented, since a and b
are oppositely oriented as boundaries of F . Note that a and b may actually coincide, in which
case the handle ha “ hb is slid over hc twice with opposite orientations.

   Let c1 denote the mid height circle of this tube, which bounds a disk D1 in Fc parallel to the
core of hc . Now c1 may or may not bound a compatibly framed disk D in B 4 ´ Fc ; in the case
pictured it does. If D exists, one can perform ambient surgery on Fc to produce a new surface
F c (read ‘F under c’) by replacing D1 with D, and represent Fc as an embedded connected
sum F c #σ S, where S is (isotopic to) the sphere D Y D1 . Here σ is an arc that guides the
tube, which can of course be moved into different positions as in the passage from the lower
right to the lower left in Figure 4.
   Recall that the connected sum F #σ S can be defined for any two disjoint, oriented surfaces
F and S in a 4-manifold Z, where σ is an embedded arc joining F to S with interior in
Z ´ pF Y Sq. This construction is independent up to isotopy of the splitting of the normal
bundle of σ one uses to specify the tube, but depends in general on the relative homotopy class
of σ (the endpoints of σ are allowed to move in F and S during the homotopy). If there is
only one such homotopy class, then we say that the connected sum, simply written F # S, is
well-defined. The following two assertions are readily verified:


   Assertion 2.1.    If Z ´ pF Y Sq is simply-connected, then F # S is well-defined.


  Assertion 2.2. If S is a sphere with trivial normal bundle and S is an oppositely oriented
pushoff of S, then pF # Sq # S is isotopic to F provided both F # S and pF # Sq # S are
well-defined.


The key stable isotopy
   Assertions 2.1 and 2.2 will be used in a key situation that arises in our proof of the
stabilization results, showing (under suitable conditions) that the surface obtained by sliding
twice with opposite orientations over a 2-handle can be pulled off the handle. Let X be the
4-ball with a 2-handle attached along a `1-framed slice knot K, and let S be the 2-sphere
of self-intersection `1 consisting of the core of the 2-handle together with a chosen slice disk
for K. We now stabilize X, viewing S Ă Z :“ X # S 2 ˆS 2 . This changes the handlebody by
adding two 2-handles, attached along a zero-framed Hopf link pa, bq. The curves a and b bound
disks in B 4 ´ S which, when capped off with the cores of ha and hb , provide a pair of dual
2-spheres A and B of self-intersection zero in Z ´ S.
Page 8 of 25                     AUCKLY, KIM, MELVIN AND RUBERMAN



  Now suppose that S appears as in the top left corner of the Figure 5 with two oppositely
oriented parallel sheets to one side of pa, bq, and a ribbon to the other.

  Sliding both sheets over ha and the ribbon over hb moves S to the sphere Saa shown in the
top right corner of the figure. As explained above, Saa decomposes as a connected sum of the
sphere T :“ S aa in X shown in the bottom right corner (obtained by sliding S under a twice
with opposite orientations) with two oppositely oriented copies of the sphere A, that is,
                                         Saa “ pT #σ Aq #τ Ā
for suitable arcs σ and τ . In fact these sums are well-defined, independent of σ and τ , by
Assertion 2.1. To see this for T #σ A, it suffices to show that the fundamental group of the
complement C “ Z ´ pT Y Aq is trivial. This group is normally generated by the meridians of
T and A, since Z is simply-connected. But the meridian of A is isotopic in C, via the dual
sphere B, to a product of (a pair of oppositely oriented) meridians of T , and so it suffices to
show that the meridian m of T is null-homotopic in C. But since T ¨ T “ 1, the normal bundle
N of T is a Hopf bundle, and so m is in fact null-homotopic in BN , and so also in C. The same
proof shows pT # Aq #τ Ā is well-defined, since T #σ A has self-intersection 1.
   Assertion 2.2 now shows that Saa is isotopic to T , which is disjoint from ha (and hb ). A
final isotopy of the Hopf link, twisting a half turn in a right-handed upward direction, gives an
alternative view of S aa in the bottom left picture.

Extending a diffeomorphism from the boundary of 4-manifold
  A crucial point for us will be to show that a diffeomorphism of the boundary of a particular
4-manifold (a blown-up cork) extends over the 4-manifold. The idea behind finding such
extensions has been known to experts [1, 56] since the mid-1970s and used many times. For the
                            STABLE ISOTOPY IN FOUR DIMENSIONS                        Page 9 of 25


reader’s convenience, we give a clear statement of the general principle; compare [6, §2.6]. To
this end, define a k-handlebody X to be a manifold with a handle decomposition with handles
of index ď k, and write X pjq for the union of handles of index ď j.
   If H is a handle of index j, then the boundary of its cocore is a sphere, called the belt sphere
of H, that acquires a natural framing as a submanifold of X pj´1q . In the case at hand, where
X has dimension 4 and j “ 2, this framed sphere is just the meridian of the attaching circle
of the handle, and in standard pictures of X would have framing 0.

   Extension Lemma 2.3. Let X be a 4-dimensional 2-handlebody and f : BX Ñ BX be
a diffeomorphism of its boundary. Choose a set L of meridians for the 2-handles, framed as
described above. Then f extends to a diffeomorphism of X if and only if the framed link
f pLq Ă BX bounds a disjoint collection of framed disks in X whose tubular neighborhood has
complement diffeomorphic to X p1q .


  Proof. View X upside down as gotten by adding 2, 3, and 4 handles to BX. Use the framings
to extend over the dual 2-handles of X rel BX. Then use Laudenbach-Poénaru [49] to extend
over the rest of X.

Stabilizing elliptic surfaces
   We use [40] as a convenient reference for complex surfaces, and in particular for the minimal
elliptic surfaces Epnq, which give rise to many of our examples. Recall from [40, 7.1.11] that
if X and X 1 are 4-manifolds containing embedded tori T and T 1 with trivial normal bundles,
then we can form the fiber sum
                             X T #T 1 X 1 “ pX ´ N q \φ pX 1 ´ N 1 q
where N and N 1 are tubular neighborhoods of T and T 1 , and φ is a bundle map between their
boundaries. In general this construction depends on φ (see e.g. [39, Example 3.2]), but not in
the situations we will encounter.
  We will use the fact that Epnq is built as a fiber sum of n copies of the rational elliptic
surface Ep1q – X1,9 . It follows easily that
             Epnq`´ – X2n,10n        (in fact it is known that Epnq` – X2n,10n´1 )
using the Mandelbaum-Moishezon trick [52, 53, 57], which states that if X, X 1 and X T #T 1 X 1
are simply-connected with X odd, then pX T #T 1 X 1 q # S 2 ˆS 2 – pX # X 1 q # 2 S 2 ˆS 2 . The
simplest proof of this uses 5-dimensional handlebody theory: X T #T 1 X 1 is the upper boundary
of ppX \ X 1 q ˆ Iq Y h where h is a ‘toral’ 1-handle, or equivalently a 1-handle, two 2-handles
and a 3-handle (cf. ‘round’ handle theory [14]). Adding the 1-handle gives X # X 1 on the
boundary, and then each 2-handle contributes an S 2 ˆS 2 factor (since X # X 1 is simply-
connected and odd). Now turning the 3-handle upside down so that it becomes a 2-handle
attached to the fiber sum gives the result (cf. [15]).


                             3. Corks in blown-up elliptic surfaces
  The work of Freedman [33] and Donaldson [26, 28] led to the discovery of many families of
exotic smooth structures on simply-connected 4-manifolds. Current methods for constructing
these include logarithmic transforms, knot surgeries, and rational blowdowns [35, 32, 31].
  We will make use of a remarkable localization of the change in smooth structure to a
contractible piece, known as a cork twist. By definition, a cork is a pair pC, τ q where C is an
oriented compact contractible 4-manifold and τ is an involution on the boundary BC that does
Page 10 of 25               AUCKLY, KIM, MELVIN AND RUBERMAN



not extend to a diffeomorphism of the full manifold (it always extends to a homeomorphism
by Freedman [33]). Given an embedding C ãÑ X, one can remove C from X and then reglue
it using τ . This is the associated cork twist, denoted
                                     X τ “ pX ´ C ˝ q Yτ C
by mild abuse of notation, as it may depend on the embedding (cf. Akbulut-Yasui [13]).
Typically X τ will not be diffeomorphic to X, and if this is the case for some embedding of C
in X then we say that pC, τ q is a cork in X, and that the embedding is effective. In general,
different embeddings of C in X are considered distinct if and only if their associated cork twists
are not diffeomorphic.

The Akbulut-Mazur cork W
  That cork twisting could change the smooth structure of a manifold was discovered by
Akbulut [2] in 1989, and it is now known that any two homeomorphic simply-connected smooth
4-manifolds differ by a single cork twist [24, 54]. In his construction, Akbulut used a specific
Mazur manifold [55, 8] W, depicted in Figure 6 from four different perspectives:


           0
                                 0                         0                 0
                                                    τ
   W “                                                         2     1           3     2




                          Figure 6. The Akbulut-Mazur cork pW, τ q


The leftmost picture is (the mirror of) Mazur’s original drawing of a pair of algebraically
canceling 1 and 2-handles, and the others are isotopic deformations of that drawing (where the
‘twist box’ ——k—   — indicates that the parallel strands entering from the left undergo k full
twists before exiting on the right). Note that the boundary of W is given by the same pictures,
where the dotted circle is replaced by a 0-framed circle. Thus the involution τ , given by a 180˝
rotation about the horizontal axis in the second picture, makes sense on the boundary, where
it interchanges the two surgery curves. Since the dotted curve is the boundary of a disk in
B 4 that has been removed, there is no obvious way to extend τ to a diffeomorphism of W,
and Akbulut showed in [2] that in fact it does not extend. The proof is to embed W in a
smooth 4-manifold X with non-trivial gauge-theoretic invariants (Akbulut used Donaldson’s
polynomial invariants, but now Seiberg-Witten invariants are typically used) in such a way
that the corresponding invariants of X τ vanish. For the reader’s convenience, here is more
detailed sketch of this argument:
   In [2], Akbulut used the blown-up elliptic surface Ep2q´ “ Ep2q # CP2 as the target of his
embedding of W. Such an embedding is transparent (following the exposition in [13]) from the
rightmost drawings of W in Figure 6 and of Ep2q´ in Figure 7. The first drawing in Figure 7
is obtained from the picture of Ep2q in Gompf and Stipsicz’s book [40, Figure 8.16] by a
handleslide (cf. Figure 3 in [13]) and a negative blowup, whose exceptional curve e appears in
the upper right corner. Sliding the `1-framed handle hc over hd and he yields the ´1-framed
handle hc1 shown in the middle drawing. Then sliding ha over hc1 produces the 2-handle ha1 in
the last drawing (where a1 is the thick figure 8) which together with the 1-handle reproduces
the last picture of W in Figure 6. Note that this embedding of W is disjoint from a copy of the
Gompf nucleus N p2q [38], given by the trefoil and its meridian in Figure 7 .

   The cork twist Ep2q´τ associated to this embedding of W can be drawn by interchanging the
dot on the 1-handle with the zero-framing on a1 , and this evidently contains an embedded `1
sphere – the core of hb capped off with a disk in B 4 – and several ´1 spheres. As a consequence,
Ep2q´τ splits off an S 2 ˆS 2 summand (in fact Ep2q´τ – X3,20 [2]) and so has vanishing Seiberg-
Witten invariants. Moreover, this summand is disjoint from the nucleus N p2q, and it follows
(as first observed by Akbulut and Yasui [13, Theorem 1.2]) that W has infinitely many distinct
cork embeddings in Ep2q´τ ; these can be constructed using knot surgeries [32] on a regular
fiber in N p2q, appealing to the fact that such surgeries are all 1-stably equivalent [4, 15].
   By a completely analogous argument it is seen that W embeds in Epnq´ for all n ě 2 (the
only change in the picture is to add more ˘1-framed 2-handles and adjust the framing to ´n on
the meridian to the trefoil, see [17, 13]) and Epnq´τ (presumably diffeomorphic to X2n´1,10n )
splits off an S 2 ˆS 2 -summand, and so has trivial Seiberg-Witten invariants. As before, there
is a Gompf nucleus N pnq disjoint from this embedding and from the S 2 ˆS 2 summand, and so
W has infinitely many distinct cork embeddings in Epnq´τ .

                4. 1-stably symmetric corks and the proofs of Theorems A and B
  We will prove our stable isotopy results by showing that the Akbulut-Mazur cork W “ C0
and the positron P “ C ´1{2 become symmetric (in a precise sense defined below) after summing
with CP2 . The argument extends with no extra effort to the families Ch and C h , and so we
have drawn the pictures for the general case.
  Given any cork pC, τ q, the boundaries of C and C ` “ C # CP2 are naturally identified, so
τ can also be viewed as an involution on BC ` . For the remainder of this section, we denote by
S the copy of CP1 in the CP2 factor of C ` .
                             STABLE ISOTOPY IN FOUR DIMENSIONS                         Page 13 of 25


   Definition. A cork pC, τ q is 1-stably symmetric if the involution τ on BC ` extends to a
smooth automorphism (still called τ ) of C ` so that the 2-spheres S and T “ τ pSq are 1-stably
isotopic, i.e. smoothly isotopic in C `# S 2 ˆS 2 .

   There is no particular reason to suppose that the extension of τ is an involution, although
it turns out to be so in the examples presented below. Our basic technique for constructing
strictly 1-stably isotopic spheres is summarized in the following theorem.


  Theorem 4.1. If pC, τ q is a 1-stably symmetric cork in a simply-connected 4-manifold X,
then the spheres S and T in C ` , regarded as submanifolds of X ` , are
  a) topologically isotopic, and
  b) strictly 1-stably isotopic, i.e. smoothly isotopic in X ` #S 2 ˆS 2 but not in X ` .
Furthermore, if pC, τ q has a family of distinct cork embeddings in X with associated cork twists
Xk , for k in some indexing set, then there is a corresponding family of topologically isotopic
spheres Sk in X ` that are pairwise strictly 1-stably isotopic.


   Proof. We sketch the standard argument for a); compare [50, 45, 65]. Since S and T are
embedded in C ` with simply-connected complements, they are homologous, from which it
follows (using Freedman [34]) that there is a self-homeomorphism of X ` taking S to T . This
homeomorphism may be assumed to be the identity on H2 pX ` q, so the theorem of Perron [59]
and Quinn [60] implies that it is topologically isotopic to the identity, yielding a topological
ambient isotopy taking S to T .
   To prove b), note that since pC, τ q is 1-stably symmetric, the spheres S and T are (smoothly)
isotopic in C `# S 2 ˆS 2 , and hence also in X `# S 2 ˆS 2 . But they are not isotopic in X ` , since
blowing down S in X ` yields X while blowing down T yields X τ :
                 X ` { T “ pX ´ C ˝ q Yid pC ` { T q
                          – pX ´ C ˝ q Yτ pC ` { Sq “ pX ´ C ˝ q Yτ C “ X τ .
Since C is a cork in X, the manifolds X ` { S and X ` { T are not diffeomorphic, so there is no
diffeomorphism of X ` taking S to T . (In principle, this is a stronger statement than saying
that S and T are not isotopic, but we don’t know an example to illustrate the difference.)
   We now prove the last assertion. By hypothesis, there are embeddings Ck Ă X of copies of C
with X τk – Xk , where τk : BCk is the involution corresponding to τ . After suitable isotopies,
                                  œ
we may assume that the intersection of the Ck ’s has nonempty interior, and a positive blowup
of a point there yields a sphere S Ă X ` of self-intersection 1 that lies in each Ck . Since C is
1-stably symmetric, τk extends over Ck` Ă X ` , and we set
                                       Sk “ τk pSq Ă X ` .
Now the argument that the Sk are topologically isotopic and pairwise strictly 1-stably isotopic
proceeds exactly as in a) and b), noting that X ` {Sk – X τk – Xk .


  Theorem 4.2. The corks Ch and C h are 1-stably symmetric.


   Proof. The arguments for Ch and for C h are effectively the same, so we will treat the former
in detail, and only briefly discuss the latter at the end of the proof.
   We first show that the involution τ on BCh extends after a positive blowup. This fact is
well known for the Akbulut-Mazur cork C0 (and implicit in [8]) but we will give a careful
argument so that we may draw the spheres, labeled Sh and Th “ τ pSh q, in a suitable picture
Page 14 of 25               AUCKLY, KIM, MELVIN AND RUBERMAN



of Ch` “ Ch # CP2 . This will allow us to explicitly construct the required isotopy between Sh
and Th in Ch` # S 2 ˆS 2 .
   Our initial picture of Ch (Figure 8) has the evident boundary involution τ given by 180˝
rotation about the midlevel horizontal axis. Our final picture of Ch` will have the analogous
boundary involution, that we continue to label τ , whose extension will be apparent from the
picture. As the bounding 3-manifolds BCh` carry more than one involution [18, 43, 47] we will
be careful to verify that the sequence of handle slides that carry one picture to the other are
τ -equivariant on the boundary, so that these involutions may be identified.
   Let Kh be the knot in S 3 drawn in Figure 12 below, and Rh be the 4-manifold obtained
from B 4 by attaching a `1 framed 2-handle along Kh . The indicated rotational symmetry τ
of Kh is induced by a linear involution of B 4 that extends in a standard fashion to Rh .


                                          h ´ 12
                                                                     τ


                                          h ´ 12


                               Figure 12. The ribbon knot Kh


Observe that Kh is a ribbon knot. In particular, it bounds two obvious immersed ribbon
disks Ah and Bh in S 3 , with τ pAh q “ Bh . These disks are drawn on the left and right side of
Figure 13 for the case when h is an integer, each appearing as a pair of stacked disks, twisted in
the middle and joined by a single ribbon. Resolving the singularities of Ah and Bh by pushing
their interiors into B 4 , and then capping off with the core of the 2-handle, we obtain a pair
of homologous embedded 2-spheres Sh and Th in Rh with Th “ τ pSh q, specified by the same
pictures by our drawing conventions.

  Lemma 4.3. There is a diffeomorphism ρ : Ch` Ñ Rh that is τ -equivariant on the boundary
and that maps S Ă Ch` to the sphere Sh Ă Rh shown on the left in Figure 13.


  Before proving the lemma, observe that it yields the desired extension of τ over Ch` . Simply
conjugate the extension of τ over Rh by ρ. Furthermore, the last assertion in the lemma shows
that the triple pRh , Sh , Th q is diffeomorphic to pCh` , S, T q, so the proof of the theorem will
be complete once we produce an isotopy between Sh and Th in Rh # S 2 ˆS 2 . To accomplish
this, we apply the ‘key stable isotopy’ shown in Figure 5 and simultaneously keep track of the
motion of Sh and Th . The stabilization adds a pair of 2-handles attached along a zero-framed
Hopf link. We then slide the `1 framed handle attached to the knot Kh four times over one
of these 2-handles, moving Kh to an unknot in S 3 , and Sh and Th to a pair of disks in S 3

bounded by this unknot, as shown in Figure 14 after a further isotopy to remove canceling
intersections of the ribbons with the stacked disks. Since any two disks bounding an unknot in
S 3 are isotopic rel boundary, this yields the desired isotopy. Note that the initial position of
each of the surfaces Sh after sliding Kh over the Hopf link is far more complicated; the point
of the isotopy in Figure 5 is to achieve the simple position shown in Figure 14.

     We can now prove our main stabilization results about spheres.

Proof of Theorem A
   By Theorem 4.2 , the Akbulut-Mazur cork W “ C0 and the positron P “ C ´1{2 are 1-stably
symmetric corks. Thus by Theorem 4.1, it suffices to show that for the stated values of p and q,
either W has infinitely many distinct cork embeddings (when p ě 4) or P has an effective cork
embedding (when p “ 2) in some 4-manifold X with X ` – Xp,q . But by [13], W has infinitely
many distinct embeddings in Epnq´τ (see Section 3), and Epnq´τ ` – Epnq´` (since τ extends
to W` ) which is diffeomorphic to X2n,10n by the Mandelbaum-Moishezon trick, as noted at
the end of Section 2. Since manifolds distinguished by their Seiberg-Witten invariants remain
distinct after summing with CP2 [30], this proves the theorem when p ě 4. Similarly by [5], P
is a cork in the Dolgachev surface Ep1q2,3 (see the end of Section 3) and Ep1q` 2,3 – X2,9 [57].
The proof for p “ 2 now follows from the blowup formula for Seiberg-Witten invariants.       ˝

Disks versus spheres
   Viewing the spheres Sh and Th in the model for the blown up cork Ch` shown in the bottom
right corner of Figure 18 provides good intuition into the result that we just proved. In this
model Sh is plainly visible, as shown in the figure, while Th will appear as the rotated image
of Sh with a pair of tubes added (capped off over the zero-framed 2-handle) to avoid the disk
bounding the dotted circle that was removed. This disk evidently obstructs the isotopy of Th
to the Sh . When one stabilizes, the effect is to change the dotted circle to a zero-framed circle.
This fills in the missing disk and the key isotopy of Section 2 may then be used.
   Even though the meridian of the disk associated to the dotted circle does not bound a smooth
embedded disk, it does bound an smoothly immersed disk D since the complement of Th is
simply-connected. Presumably D can be used to construct a Casson handle, which in turn can
be used to construct a topological isotopy between the pair of spheres.
Page 18 of 25               AUCKLY, KIM, MELVIN AND RUBERMAN



  One may wonder if this behavior already takes place at the level of the two ribbon disks
Ah and Bh for the knot Kh shown in Figure 13, i.e. these disks are distinct, but perhaps they
become isotopic after stabilizing with S 2 ˆS 2 . The answer is no. This is shown in the following
proposition, and demonstrates the need for care when performing stabilization by replacing a
dotted circle by a zero framed circle.


  Proposition 4.4. The two ribbon disks Ah , Bh Ă B 4 for Kh remain non-isotopic relative
to the boundary after any number of stabilizations of B 4 . In fact, for any simply-connected
4-manifold X, no (smooth) automorphism of B 4 # X extending the identity on the boundary
will carry Ah to Bh .


  Proof. Assume to the contrary that such an automorphism φ of B 4 # X exists. We will
show by fundamental group considerations that this leads to a contradiction.
  Recall that the involution τ of B 4 (introduced in the discussion above Figure 12) swaps the
disks Ah and Bh . After an isotopy, we may assume that τ leaves fixed a small 4-ball away from
Kh , and use this to construct an automorphism τ # idX of B 4 # X that swaps Ah and Bh (see
Section 5). Now consider the composition

                           ρ “ pτ # idX q ˝ ϕ : B 4 # X Ñ B 4 # X.

This diffeomorphism preserves Ah (setwise) and restricts to τ on the boundary S 3 , inducing an
automorphism ρ˚ of π1 pB 4 # X ´ Ah q “ π1 pB 4 ´ Ah q (by the Seifert-Van Kampen Theorem)
that restricts to τ˚ on π1 pS 3 ´ Kh q. But this is impossible, as we now show.
   The first step is to construct a handle decomposition of the complement of an open tubular
neighborhood N pAh q of Ah in B 4 , following the standard technique [56, 9, 40]. Start with the
picture of Kh from Figure 12 , reproduced on the left side of Figure 21 . Note that the curves a
and b shown there are swapped by τ . Now B 4 ´ N pAh q is obtained from a small 4-ball about
the origin by adding an pi ` 1q-handle for each i-handle in Ah associated to any critical level
embedding, and so in our case we have two 1-handles and one 2-handle, as shown in the middle
picture in Figure 21. This picture is redrawn after an isotopy on the right side of the figure,
also tracking the a and b curves through this process.


a                                  a
             h ´ 12                              h ´ 12

                                                                          a            2h ´ 12

             h ´ 12                              h ´ 12
b                                   b                                                            b
                        Figure 21. Complement of the ribbon disk Ah


    One can now read off a presentation of the fundamental group of the complement of Ah

                             π1 pB 4 ´ Ah q “ x x, y | xy “ pyxq2 y

and observe that a “ xy and b “ 1. By hypothesis ρ˚ paq is conjugate to b, so xy “ 1. But this
group has a representation onto the symmetric group S3 mapping x to p1 2q and y to p2 3q, and
so xy to p1 2 3q, a contradiction.
                              STABLE ISOTOPY IN FOUR DIMENSIONS                          Page 19 of 25


  Remark. This fundamental group calculation is specific to the family of corks Ch . In
contrast, the complements of the ribbon disks associated to the positron cork P and its
generalizations C h (given by the same picture but with 2h in the twist box) have fundamental
group x x, y | xy “ x2 y 2 y – Z. These disks are topologically equivalent but smoothly distinct,
and give rise to the phenomenon that Akbulut calls [6, §10.2] (see also [3][7]) an ‘anti-cork’.
We do not know if they are 1-stably isotopic.

Brunnian links and the proof of Theorem B
   A non-trivial link in the sphere all of whose proper sublinks are trivial is called Brunnian [20,
25]. The notion has an obvious extension to links in arbitrary manifolds; one might look for
families of inequivalent links with equivalent proper sublinks. As in Section 1 , we call such
a family Brunnian. Here we prove Theorem B , asserting the existence of Brunnian families
of m-component links for any m ě 2 in suitable completely decomposable 4-manifolds, using
Theorem 4.2.
   We first construct Brunnian pairs pL, M q. Start with a 1-stably symmetric cork C in
4-manifold X, and assume that C is also a cork in X # 2 CP2 . By the blowup formula,
this is automatically the case whenever X and X τ are distinguished by Seiberg-Witten or
Donaldson invariants. The spheres S and T in C ` Ă X ` yield links L “ pS, S2 , . . . , Sm q and
M “ pT, S2 , . . . , Sm q in Z “ X ` # pm ´ 1q CP2 # 2 CP2 , where S2 , . . . , Sm are the exceptional
spheres in the CP2 ’s. Evidently L and M are smoothly distinct, since Z{L “ X ´´ , Z{M “
X τ ´´ , and Z{L fl Z{M because C is a cork in X ´´ . Since twisting is not seen topologically,
L and M are topologically isotopic.
   To prove the Brunnian property, it suffices by symmetry to show that the proper sublinks
L1 “ pS, S2 , . . . , Sm´1 q and M 1 “ pT, S2 , . . . , Sm´1 q are isotopic in Z. Grouping the last three
summands in Z with X ` , we view Z “ X ``´´ #pm ´ 2q CP2 with S and T lying in X ``´´ “
X ` # S 2 ˆS 2 # CP2 and S2 , . . . , Sk lying in pm ´ 2qCP2 . The 1-stable symmetry of C implies
that S and T are isotopic in X ``´´ , whence L1 and M 1 are isotopic in Z.
   To get the statement of Theorem B, suppose first that p “ 2n with n ě 2. If we choose X to
be the blown-up elliptic surface Epnq´ , and use the Akbulut-Mazur cork W in the construction
described above, we have Z – Xp`m´1,5p`2 . Values of q ą 5p ` 2 result from blowing up Epnq´
an arbitrary number of times. If n “ 1, then we would choose X to be the Dolgachev surface,
and let C be the positron cork P in X. The construction then produces a Brunnian pair in
Xm`1,11 , and by blowing up X, in Xm`1,q for any q ě 11.
   As in Theorem A, the fact that W has infinitely many distinct cork embeddings in a
4-manifold X with X` – X2n,10n leads to infinite Brunnian families.                                   ˝

                       5. 1-stable isotopy of diffeomorphisms and psc metrics
   As mentioned in the introduction, a sphere Σ of self-intersection ˘1 in a 4-manifold Z gives
rise to a self-diffeomorphism ρΣ of Z that induces ‘reflection in rΣs ’ on H2 pZq, and isotopic
spheres yield isotopic diffeomorphisms. (This diffeomorphism is just the connected sum of the
identity on the complement of the sphere with complex conjugation acting on a neighborhood
of the sphere in ˘CP2 .) The sequence of papers [61, 62, 63] uses that observation to construct
interesting self-diffeomorphisms as follows: Start with a sphere S of self-intersection `1 in a
simply-connected 4-manifold X, and consider the self-diffeomorphism
                                     fS “ ρS`E1 `E2 ˝ ρS´E1 `E2
of Z “ X # 2 CP , where E1 and E2 are the exceptional spheres in the CP2 factors. Here
                   2

the ˘ signs indicate connected sums of the spheres, preserving or reversing orientation as
appropriate. Since these spheres have simply-connected complements, the sums are well-defined
Page 20 of 25               AUCKLY, KIM, MELVIN AND RUBERMAN



by Assertion 2.1. Now suppose that T is another sphere of self-intersection `1 in X, and that
b`
 2 pXq is even and at least 4. If S and T are homologous, then the diffeomorphisms fS and fT
are topologically isotopic [59, 60], but it is shown in [61] that they are not smoothly isotopic
if X{S and X{T are distinguished by some Seiberg-Witten or Donaldson invariant.
   As we have seen above, we can choose the manifolds X and Z amongst the Xp,q , and
(with suitable restrictions on p and q) get infinitely many spheres, resulting in infinitely many
isotopy classes of diffeomorphisms. Theorem C asserts that the resulting diffeomorphisms are
all isotopic after a single stabilization. We actually prove a somewhat sharper statement, which
concerns the behavior of the group π0 pDiff pM qq of isotopy classes of (orientation preserving)
diffeomorphisms of M under stabilization. The issue is that connected sum is not, a priori,
a well-defined operation on isotopy classes of self-diffeomorphisms. In a technical section that
follows this one, we will show that that for a simply-connected M 4 , connected sum with the
identity on ˘CP2 or S 2 ˆS 2 is in fact well-defined. As a corollary, we find a well-defined
homomorphism Φ : π0 pDiff pM qq Ñ π0 pDiff pM # S 2 ˆS 2 q, and prove via Theorem C that its
kernel is infinite.

   Proof Proof of Theorem C. For even p ě 4 and q ě 5p ` 2, the proof of Theorem A yields
an infinite family of topologically isotopic spheres Si of self-intersection `1 in Xp,q´2 that
are not smoothly isotopic, distinguished by the Seiberg-Witten invariants of their blow-downs
Xp,q´2 {Si , but that become smoothly isotopic in Xp,q´2 # S 2 ˆS 2 – Xp`1,q´1 . The results of
[61] (discussed above) show that the self-diffeomorphisms fSi : Xp,q Ñ Xp,q are pairwise non-
isotopic. Since the Si are isotopic in Xp`1,q´1 , the spheres Si ˘ E1 ` E2 , and consequently the
diffeomorphisms fSi , are isotopic in Xp`1,q`1 – Xp,q # S 2 ˆS 2 , as asserted.

   We turn now to the proof of Theorem D . The Xp,q admit metrics of positive scalar curvature
(PSC) constructed as connected sums [41, 64] of standard metrics on ˘CP2 . For a generic PSC
metric gp,q on Xp,q , it was shown in [63] that the metrics fS˚i gp,q are mutually non-isotopic.
We want to show that these become isotopic after a single stabilization.
   The notion of stabilization of metrics runs into the same issue of well-definedness (even up
to isotopy) as we encountered in the case of diffeomorphisms. In order to perform a connected
sum of PSC metrics on manifolds X and Y one typically deforms the metrics (maintaining the
PSC condition) in a neighborhood of points x in X and y in Y into a standard form (a ‘torpedo
metric’ [69]) after which they can be glued by identifying X and Y away from x and y. The
issue of whether the resulting metric on X # Y is well-defined (independent up to isotopy of all
choices in the construction) can be addressed in a fashion similar to Section 5 , using techniques
in [70]. However, to avoid an unnecessary technical discussion, we fix a PSC metric on S 2 ˆS 2
containing a torpedo region, and a metric gp,q on each Xp,q with such a region disjoint from the
spheres used to make the diffeomorphisms fSi . As explained in the introduction, Theorem D
then follows from Theorem C.

Stabilizing diffeomorphisms
   We now address the technical issue of well-definedness of stabilization of diffeomorphisms
under connected sum. A basic theorem in differential topology [44, Chapter 8], going back
to Palais [58] states that any two orientation preserving embeddings of an n-disk D in an
oriented n-manifold M are smoothly isotopic. (We assume throughout that all manifolds are
connected.) This implies that the connected sum of oriented manifolds is well-defined up to
diffeomorphism.
   Now, given two diffeomorphisms f : M Ñ M and f 1 : M 1 Ñ M 1 , each restricting to the
identity on embedded disks D and D1 , we can form the connected sum
                                 f # f1 : M # M1 Ñ M # M1
                            STABLE ISOTOPY IN FOUR DIMENSIONS                      Page 21 of 25


as follows. In the interior of each of D and D1 , fix smaller disks D0 and D01 , and specify
                            M # M 1 “ pM ´ D0 q YB pM 1 ´ D01 q
with f # f 1 defined to restrict to f and f 1 respectively on the two halves. Note that f # f 1
depends, up to isotopy, only on f and f 1 considered up to isotopy relative to D0 and D01 .
   Suppose now that f is an arbitrary orientation-preserving diffeomorphism and f 1 “ idM 1 .
By Palais’ theorem, f can be isotoped to a diffeomorphism g that is the identity on a disk,
and it might seem that we can define f # f 1 to be g # f 1 . We would like to say that this is a
well-defined operation on isotopy classes; in other words, that it does not depend on the choice
of isotopy between f and g. This is a well-known issue in the study of the mapping class group
of surfaces, where there are stabilization results for mapping class groups of diffeomorphisms
that are the identity on the boundary [42], but not for the mapping class groups of closed
surfaces.
   For example, take M and M 1 to be genus 2 surfaces, with f “ idM and the isotopy from f
to g to be one that drags a disk around an essential closed loop γ Ă M . Then f # f 1 would be
represented by a composition of Dehn twists (with opposite senses) around a pair of homologous
but non-isotopic curves, and hence would not be isotopic to the identity. Similarly, one might
vary f by an isotopy from the identity to itself that rotates the disk D by a non-trivial element
of π1 pSOp2qq. Again, standard examples show that this operation can change the connected
sum of diffeomorphisms by a Dehn twist around a separating curve on a surface.
   In contrast, we will show that for simply-connected 4-manifolds, there is a well-defined (up
to isotopy) assignment pf, f 1 q ÞÑ f # f 1 when M 1 is ˘CP2 or S 2 ˆS 2 and f 1 is the identity
diffeomorphism. First, we collect some standard results about diffeomorphism groups, using
the following notation. For the moment M will denote an oriented closed smooth n-manifold
with a fixed embedding of an n-disk D. Then we have the following spaces, each with the C 8
topology:
   – Diff pM q is the group of orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms of M
   – Diff D pM q consists of diffeomorphisms whose restriction to D is the identity
   – EmbpD, M q is the space of orientation preserving embeddings of D in M
Finally, FpM q will denote the bundle of oriented (not necessarily orthonormal) frames in the
tangent bundle. As such, it is a fiber bundle over M with fiber GL`  n pRq The following facts are
well-known to experts; the first is proved using parameterized versions of the isotopy extension
and tubular neighborhood theorems [22, 44], while the second is a parameterized version of
the Cerf-Palais disk embedding theorem [22, 58]


  Lemma 5.1. With the notation above,
  a) Restricting a diffeomorphism to D defines a fiber bundle Diff pM q Ñ EmbpD, M q
     with fiber Diff D pM q
  b) The differential at 0 P D of an embedding defines a homotopy equivalence
     EmbpD, M q Ñ FpM q.
  An element in π1 pSOpnqq, viewed as a smooth path beginning and ending at the identity, pro-
duces a diffeomorphism of S n´1 ˆ I. If S n´1 ˆ I is embedded in M , then this diffeomorphism
extends naturally to M ; we refer to such a diffeomorphism as a Dehn twist.


   Proposition 5.2. Let M be a simply-connected n-manifold, and fix disks D0 Ă D Ă M .
Let f : M Ñ M be an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism. Then there a diffeomorphism
g : M Ñ M isotopic to f that is the identity on D. Any two choices of g differ up to isotopy
relative to D0 by composition of Dehn twists supported in D ´ intpD0 q.
Page 22 of 25                AUCKLY, KIM, MELVIN AND RUBERMAN



   The composition could mean no Dehn twists, in which case the two choices are isotopic. We
remind the reader that for n ě 3, since π1 pSOpnqq – Z2 , the composition of such a Dehn twist
with itself is isotopic to the identity.
   Proof. The existence of such a diffeomorphism g follows, as mentioned above, from an
isotopy of D to f pDq. Two choices of g defined by such isotopies differ (up to isotopy of M )
by an element of π1 pDiff pM qq, which is of course an isotopy of idM to itself. Combine the two
parts of Lemma 5.1 and consider the homotopy long exact sequence of the fibration:
      π1 pDiff D0 pM qq      / π1 pDiff pM qq     / π1 pEmbpD0 , M qq       / π0 pDiff D0 pM qq

                                                             –
                                                            
                                                       π1 pFpM qq
   From this we see that the obstruction to lifting this to an isotopy of idM to itself, relative to
D0 , comes from an element of π1 pFpM qq. But since M is simply-connected, there is a surjection
π1 pSOpnqq Ñ π1 pFpM qq. This implies the last statement of the proposition.


  Theorem 5.3. Let f : M Ñ M be an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism of a simply-
connected 4-manifold. Then for X “ ˘CP2 or S 2 ˆS 2 , there is a well-defined stabilization
f # idX that depends up to isotopy only on the isotopy class of f .

   Proof. As suggested above, we isotope f to a diffeomorphism that is the identity on an
embedded disk D, and use it to define f # idX . By Proposition 5.2 the resulting diffeomorphism
of M # X is well-defined, possibly up to Dehn twists supported on an S 3 ˆ I region separating
the two summands. We claim (compare [36, Theorem 2.4]) that for X as indicated in the
theorem, such a Dehn twist is isotopic to the identity. To see this, consider an S 1 action on X
with a fixed point p; assume for convenience that it acts isometrically. The local representation
of S 1 on Tp X defines a map S 1 Ñ SOp4q. In the case of ˘CP2 and S 2 ˆS 2 , there is an action
such that this map is the generator of π1 pSOp4qq. Using this action, it is easy to find an isotopy,
supported on X, between a Dehn twist and the identity.

   Theorem 5.3 can be rephrased in terms of the group Diff pM q of (orientation-preserving)
diffeomorphisms of M .


  Corollary 5.4. Let M 4 be simply-connected. Stabilization with the identity diffeomor-
phism of X “ ˘CP2 or S 2 ˆS 2 gives a well-defined homomorphism
                             Φ : π0 pDiff pM qq Ñ π0 pDiff pM #Xqq.
For M “ Xp,q as in Theorem C and X “ S 2 ˆS 2 , the kernel of Φ is infinite.


  Proof. That Φ is well-defined is the content of Theorem 5.3. Recall that the multiplication
in π0 pGq for any topological group G is induced from the multiplication in G. Now given f0
and g0 in Diff pM q, we choose isotopies ft , gt with f1 , g1 the identity on an embedded disk D.
Then ft ˝ gt gives an isotopy of f0 ˝ g0 to f1 ˝ g1 , which is evidently also the identity on D.
Since
                            pf1 ˝ g1 q # idX “ pf1 # idX q ˝ pg1 # idX q
we see that Φprf0 srg0 sq “ Φprf1 srg1 sq “ Φprf1 sqΦprg1 sq, so that Φ is a homomorphism. Using
the same notation as in the proof of Theorem C, we see that for i ě 2, the diffeomorphisms
fSi ˝ pfS1 q´1 form an infinite subset in the kernel of Φ.
